Cleo estimates that late and incomplete deliveries cost U.S. and Canadian consumer packaged goods (CPG) and food and beverage manufacturers about $100 billion a year. The supply chain software company released the figure Tuesday in a report on on-time, in-full (OTIF) performance.
Direct costs such as retailer chargebacks, expedited freight and dispute management make up $10 billion to $11 billion of that total, according to The $100 Billion Supply Chain Penalty: OTIF’s Total Economic Impact . Cleo attributes the other $85 billion to $90 billion to losses that rarely appear in financial reporting: lost shelf space, smaller retailer orders, excess inventory and manufacturing inefficiencies.
Retailers fine suppliers when orders miss the delivery window or arrive short. Walmart requires suppliers to deliver on time and in full on 98% of orders or pay a fine of 3% of the cost of goods, when the retailer tightened its standard in 2020 .
“A missed delivery can cost a manufacturer its next order, its shelf space, and ultimately its standing with a retailer. The chargeback captures only a fraction of that damage,” Cleo President and CEO Mahesh Rajasekharan said in the rele ase .
How retailer OTIF programs work
Walmart’s U.S. OTIF program began in July 2017 , and Amazon and Target have similar standards, according to the 2020 FreightWaves article. Retailers do not measure OTIF the same way. A 2019 McKinsey study found no standard industry definition.
Cleo’s report counts a delivery as successful only if it arrives by the agreed date or within the delivery window and contains the full quantity ordered. It says retailers including Walmart, Kroger, Target, Costco and Publix set thresholds often above 95%, while industry benchmarks put many manufacturers at 85% to 91%.
A supplier at 99% against a 95% requirement generally earns no extra financial benefit, according to the report, while one at 94% can face chargebacks and lower scorecard ratings. Strong performers can win better shelf placement or promotional support, but the report says those benefits are rarely written into contracts, so suppliers often invest only enough to meet the minimum.
Most of Cleo’s $100 billion estimate comes from what follows a miss. Retailers use supplier performance to decide shelf placement, promotions and order allocation, the report says, so a weaker scorecard can shrink a supplier’s future business.
Larger suppliers pay more in penalties
Cleo’s model shows direct costs rising as a share of revenue with company size. They run 0.5% to 1% of revenue for manufacturers with $100 million to $500 million in sales and 2.5% to 3% for those with $3 billion to $5 billion. Indirect costs move the other way, from 15% to 16% of revenue at the small end to 10% to 11% at the top.
Midsize manufacturers, with $300 million to $1 billion in revenue, face the greatest risk-adjusted exposure, the report says, because they carry high indirect costs and fast-rising direct penalties.
Freight costs peak in the fourth quarter
Cleo estimates that 40% of expedited shipments happen in the fourth quarter, when promotional and holiday demand peaks. Between 5% and 15% of shipments to major retailers need expedited logistics, the report says.
Many OTIF failures start before a truck is loaded. Inaccurate forecasts, purchase orders sent late and promotional spikes push suppliers into expedited shipping or last-minute production changes, according to the report.
Air freight costs five to 10 times the standard rate, team drivers 1.5 to two times and less-than-truckload consolidation two to three times, according to Cleo. Suppliers should lock in capacity reservations and carrier commitments 90 to 120 days before the fourth quarter, the report advises.
What chargeback disputes cost
Cleo puts annual spending on chargeback disputes at $1.16 billion across the U.S. and Canadian CPG industry, covering deduction analysts, compliance managers, third-party platforms and recovery consultants.
Citing industry estimates, the report says 60% to 70% of disputed chargebacks are written off, and 20% to 30% of successful recoveries can go to recovery-service fees. It puts the fully loaded cost of a deduction analyst dedicated to a single retail channel at $80,000 to $120,000 a year.
Cleo’s recommendations
The report estimates that a 5- to 10-percentage-point improvement in OTIF performance could recover $11 billion to $23 billion across the market. It recommends that manufacturers measure direct and indirect OTIF costs together and give one executive with profit-and-loss responsibility ownership of the total.
Of the five approaches the report weighs, dispute-recovery and reporting tools require limited investment but do little about root causes. Logistics technology such as routing optimization and carrier visibility can significantly reduce on-time failures but may leave demand-planning problems unresolved, it says.
Cleo sells software in another of the five, supply chain orchestration. In February it launched Chargeback Prevention , which flags orders, shipments and invoices at risk of missing trading-partner service levels. The release says the research draws on industry benchmarks, publicly documented retailer programs, labor and logistics cost data, and scenario-based modeling.
Organizational fragmentation is the most common failure in OTIF programs, according to the report.
“The deeper problem is fragmented accountability: logistics tracks delivery performance, finance tracks deductions, and sales tracks lost business, while the connections between them go unaddressed,” Rajasekharan said. “CEOs need to make OTIF a shared business priority, with clear ownership of its full financial impact.”
Why it matters: Cleo’s estimate places about 90% of the cost of missed retail deliveries outside the chargebacks suppliers track, in lost shelf space, orders and inventory. The figures come from modeling by a company that sells chargeback-prevention software.

source_document.body:
Redwood Materials and Rivian are expanding their existing EV battery partnership, adding a fresh battery material recycling effort to the EV startup’s Normal, Illinois, vehicle factory and, potentially, other Rivian-owned sites.
As Tesla co-founder JB Straubel’s second act, Redwood Materials had a lot to live up to. Its plan to give used EV batteries a second life as energy storage for public- and private-sector buildings, construction sites, micro-grids, and (sigh) data centers makes plenty of sense, though. Enough sense, anyway, that Rivian decided to put the idea to work as it built out its R2 production line at the former Diamond-Star Mitsubishi plant in Normal. Back in April , the upstart EV brand signed on for 10 MWh worth of energy storage using repurposed Rivian battery packs – but that deal was just the beginning.
The new, expanded partnership between the two companies will see Redwood collect, sort, and recycle Rivian’s battery production scrap materials, putting them safely back into the manufacturing process with minimal waste and at a fraction of the cost of virgin material. What’s more, the new deal will see retired Rivian batteries put to use in other stationary energy projects before eventually recycling some 99% of those batteries’ critical materials (nickel, cobalt, copper, and lithium).
With the recent launch of what is sure to be the more popular , more affordable R2, that’s suddenly a much bigger deal than it might have been last year.

As the demand and cost for energy keep rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges.”
Rivian is the latest major EV brand to enter into a formal battery recycling partnership with Redwood, with the list of others including BMW, Ford, Toyota, and Volvo.

Audi Cars Are the First in the World to No Longer Need a Smartphone to Run Spotify
8 photos
Photo: Audi
Smartphones and the ability of cars to integrate them into the driving experience have completely changed the way humans move around. From navigation apps to music libraries, everything the phone has to offer has been available in cars for years, be it through a wired connection or a wireless one. But now we're living through a revolution of the infotainment system.
For a while now, the makers of various apps have started pondering the idea of offering their products to drivers in a more direct fashion, cutting the smartphone out of the equation. Simply put, they have begun adapting their apps to run in a vehicle environment, piggybacking on operating systems such as Android Automotive.
The latest name to join the trend is audio streaming platform Spotify , which, taking advantage of the Google OS expanding its reach, is launching its first-ever full in-car native app. And German carmaker Audi is the first in the world to benefit from that.
The brand with four rings announced this week that, starting October 21, 2026, the native Spotify app is making its way into certain Audi vehicles, operating directly through their infotainment system, without the need to connect a smartphone.
Just like when it comes to the mobile app, Spotify for cars will be capable of playing music (including videos), displaying real-time lyrics, and running the Spotify Jam feature. What's interesting about this is that Jam will automatically adjust itself based on whether the car is being driven or not in a bid to eliminate distraction.
For instance, it is only when the ride is parked that the full feature set and expanded browsing become available on the car's display.
For now, the Spotify in-car app will launch via the Audi Application Store on the models based on the Premium Platform Electric (PPE) and Premium Platform Combustion (PPC) architectures, meaning the likes of A6 e-tron, Q6 e-tron, A5, Q5, and A6.
The cars the feature will roll out to are all model year 2026, and will be joined later on by the upcoming Q7 and Q9. The new Spotify app will roll out in all of Audi's key markets, on six continents and in some 47 countries.
To some of you, the idea of an in-car Spotify app could seem uninteresting. I mean, it involves downloading the thing, installing it, and, naturally, logging in with the appropriate account. Yet, the experience of using Spotify should be different from how people are used to from using a smartphone connection.
For one, Audi promises a more comprehensive interface that doesn't necessarily use the standardized layouts and controls, but also a broader range of supported content – although, at the moment, it's unclear what that means.
Because it's native to the car, the Spotify app can run on multiple screens – for instance, it can remain available on the front passenger display while the vehicle is in motion.
As with all apps, downloading Spotify into your Audi doesn't cost anything, and neither does listening to music, as long as you don't mind being interrupted by ads. No matter how you do this, though, the app does need an account to run.

This Pedal-Powered RV Is Small and Light, Yet Tough Enough to Do Burning Man
22 photos
Photo: YouTube/Attoparsec
The modern society is driven by consumerism, which, in turn, is driven mostly by artificially created needs, and that's exactly the opposite of what Burning Man stands for. So what better way to make a return to Black Rock City than with a DIY project that's half functional product and half art installation?
That's an accurate description for the Bike RV, a pedal-powered DIY shelter on wheels built almost from scratch by Matthew "Fish" Dockery, best known as Attoparsec on YouTube. Dockery is a Seattle-based fabricator and artist who takes pride in his "radically impractical" builds, whether they are machinery, gadgets, or kinetic sculptures.
In 2026, he decided to return to Burning Man after a hiatus of 10 full years, and to do so with a build that would serve as shelter and means of transportation around the City in the Black Rock Desert in Nevada. He called that build the Bike RV, though perhaps a better description would be a pedal-powered shelter of the kind that are so popular at the community and art festival.
He documented the build and the following adventure at Burning Man in a video he posted on his channel, which you will find in full at the bottom of the page. It's not the kind of tutorial that will give you real-life advice or information you can use in your own build , but it's an interesting inside look at the culture of Burning Man.
Photo: YouTube/Attoparsec It's an alternative solution to millions of DIY builds that populate the online world, built with functionality in mind and very little concern to comfort. The Bike RV is a basic shelter in the manner of the hexayurt that inspired it, so it's low-cost, rapidly deployable, and surprisingly tough.
More importantly, it's all these things in a tutorial where storytelling takes center stage. To paraphrase a highly rated comment, it's a video where you come for the Bike RV and stay for Dockery's storytelling skills.
The build started with a heavy-duty cargo trike of an unknown make and brand, with a bent rear wheel and a single brake line that ironically rendered braking impossible. Dockery calls it the "most unpleasant riding experience I've ever had" after his first test ride, whose "very existence was morally offensive," and he sets out to fix the issues to have a solid base for the weight he'd end up adding.
Photo: YouTube/Attoparsec He also added a differential built with a ready-made kit to allow turning, since that had provenvirtually impossible on the test ride, and gave the trike a full paintjob to cover the existing mint green one.
Using tubular aluminum, he built a frame extension that would hold the future construction , which he imagined as a sort of capsule room, but on wheels. He'd later realize his mistake in not moving the axle farther to the rear of the trike, since the added weight posed a serious danger of tipping the whole thing over when he was inside.
He compensated for that with a pair of trailer jacks, which added stability to the rear-heavy rig. With the base of the RV on risers, he was left with lots of cargo space between frame and base, so he decided to use that to add a 12V Euhomy fridge on sliders, running off a 200W Jackery solar system he'd bought the summer before.
Photo: YouTube/Attoparsec The structure was built with 1-inch (2.5-cm) polyisocyanurate foam insulation panels held together with fiberglass tape, with the edges covered in aluminum so the foam interior wouldn't crumble away. Dockery speaks of interior lights and a modular interior, but he doesn't show any footage from inside, with the sole exception of his view of the raw panels lying down.
The construction was based on the H8 Danger Ranger hexayurt design, measuring 8 feet (2.4 meters) in length and 4 feet (1.2 meters) in width. He opted to transport it with the roof removed in the back of a U-Haul truck and have it assembled on site.
Invented in 2002 by Vinay Gupta, a hexayurt is an open-source temporary shelter in various configurations, imagined as a fast, cheap, and environmentally-friendly housing solution for disaster relief. Hexayurts are a common sight at Burning Man, so the Bike RV fit right in.
Photo: YouTube/Attoparsec So, with this rushed construction, Dockery headed out to Burning Man, where he set up camp after securing the roof of the Bike RV with long straps. He found that moving across the Playa was smooth, though not necessarily fast or effortless, and was able to enjoy his first day even though he had to stop frequently to hammer in the wheel that kept sliding off the axle.
Though most attendees now used e-bikes to move across the City, Dockery was satisfied with his solution, as heavy and faulty as it was. It proved even more useful on the second night, when a powerful storm and strong rains set in.
He eventually had to move into the back of the U-Haul truck when the Bike RV started showing signs of water ingress, and eventually packed up and left when the road dried. Still, he appreciated how the structure handled a full night of battering winds and scattered rain, despite the fact that it was not up to his construction (and artistic) standards.
Photo: YouTube/Attoparsec Dockery's conclusion is that Burning Man is no longer his scene, but he doesn't regret this final piece of functional art he created to attend this year.

Tesla has lowered its 2026 capital spending forecast. In its Q3 10-Q, the company now says it expects capital expenditures “to be in excess of $20 billion in 2026,” down from the “more than $25 billion” it had guided since April.
The change was in the 10-Q Tesla filed Wednesday, not in the shareholder letter it released the same day. And it lands in a quarter where Tesla reported $1.53 billion of positive free cash flow, a number that depends a lot on timing.
Tesla’s 2026 capex guidance keeps moving
Tesla started 2026 guiding to about $20 billion in capex. In April, it raised that to more than $25 billion, and in July, CFO Vaibhav Taneja reiterated the figure while Elon Musk called 2026 a “massive capex year.”
Now it’s back to “in excess of $20 billion.”
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Tesla has spent $13.01 billion so far this year: $2.49 billion in Q1, $5.79 billion in Q2 and $4.73 billion in Q3. Hitting $25 billion would have required about $12 billion in Q4 alone, more than double its biggest quarter. The new floor only requires about $7 billion.
The 10-Q says 2026 spending is “driven by our SI initiatives, including investments in compute infrastructure and data centers,” along with factory ramps and Tesla’s fleet of “company-operated SI-enabled assets.”
There’s a catch in the cash numbers, though. Tesla had $3.67 billion of equipment and construction spending sitting in liabilities at the end of September, meaning it was booked but not yet paid. That’s up from $2.63 billion at the end of June and $1.63 billion a year ago. So Tesla’s actual spending is running ahead of the cash capex it reports.
Where Tesla’s Q3 free cash flow came from
Tesla reported $6.26 billion in operating cash flow and $1.53 billion in free cash flow after capex. Here’s how it got there:
Q3 2026 | Amount
Net income | $0.80B
Depreciation, amortization and impairment | +$1.85B
Stock-based compensation | +$1.17B
Other non-cash items (FX, taxes, bitcoin, SpaceX) | -$0.15B
Changes in working capital | +$2.59B
Operating cash flow | $6.26B
Capital expenditures | -$4.73B
Free cash flow | $1.53B
Depreciation and stock compensation are normal add-backs. They reduce profit without using cash.
The working capital line is the one to watch. Without that $2.59 billion, Tesla’s free cash flow would have been about negative $1.06 billion.
Most of it came from bills Tesla hasn’t paid yet. Accounts payable rose $1.92 billion in the quarter and accrued liabilities rose $1.95 billion, including $722 million more in “accrued purchases,” goods Tesla received but hadn’t been invoiced for.
Another $1.26 billion came from deferred revenue, mostly energy storage. Tesla’s energy deferred revenue jumped to $3.30 billion from $2.31 billion. But not all of that is cash. Tesla disclosed that it billed SpaceX $588 million for Megapacks “that have not been delivered,” which SpaceX hadn’t paid at quarter-end. That amount sits in both deferred revenue and accounts receivable, which rose $565 million.
Those gains were partly offset by a $1.82 billion increase in prepaid expenses and other assets, and a small inventory build.
If you also count the $1.03 billion increase in unpaid capex, Tesla’s free cash flow on an “as spent” basis was closer to $500 million.
Tesla’s borrowing plans
The capex cut comes a month after Tesla signed $30 billion of new credit facilities . The 10-Q details them: a $20 billion delayed-draw term loan maturing in 2029, and $10 billion of revolving credit replacing a $5 billion facility. Tesla hadn’t drawn on either at quarter-end, and it had $45.4 billion in cash and investments.
Electrek’s Take
None of this is improper in today’s accounting standards, which we can argue are pretty awful. Paying suppliers later, collecting deposits, and booking capex when it’s incurred are all somewhat normal accounting, and Tesla disclosed them. But they explain why the “$1.5 billion of free cash flow” headline from Wednesday’s results says less about the business than it seems.
Underneath, Tesla made $718 million of operating income, less than its $1.17 billion in stock compensation, and before working capital, it burned cash. The timing items that helped this quarter will reverse when the invoices come due and the Megapacks ship.
The capex cut is the more interesting signal. Six months ago, Tesla was telling investors 2026 would be a massive spending year to build out AI compute, Optimus and Cybercab. Now it’s lowering the target in its 10-Q instead of the shareholder letter, while lining up $30 billion of debt. Either projects are slipping into 2027, or Tesla is spending less to protect its cash. Tesla should say which.

New Ferrari Luce EV Coming Stateside From $560,800
9 photos
Photo: Ferrari / edited
Made in Maranello, the first-ever Ferrari with electric-only propulsion is naturally coming stateside. According to Car and Driver, prospective customers in the US will have to spend $560,800 at the very least for the five-seater Fezza.
Enormous, isn't it? Thing is, Ferrari could have been greedier. Nearly $120,000 pricier than the Purosangue, the Luce also has rear doors and proper back seats. Any other similarity doesn't really matter, for the Luce targets very different customers who lean more into techy stuff than V12s and motorsports.
When the Luce broke cover, the cited publication expected a starting price in the ballpark of $640,000 when converting from euros. The official sticker is nearly $80,000 under that projection, yet Ferrari's newcomer still clears the Rolls-Royce Cullinan. While it may have been developed with BMW money, ultra-luxury SUVs don't get better than said British colossus from Goodwood.
Touted as the priciest five-seat vehicle for 2027, the Ferrari Luce is more attention magnet for all the wrong reasons than Prancing Horse that will be fondly remembered in a decade's time. Certain peeps believe that what hides underneath the sheetmetal is a technological flex, but Chinese automakers like Denza can do much better for less than $175,000 when converting from yuan.
Instead of the Purosangue's twelve cylinders, four electric motors are on the menu here. That's one per wheel, and their combined output is 1,035 mechanical horsepower. If you know your high-performance BEVs well, that means the Luce is only 16 ponies up on the lower-slung Porsche Taycan Turbo GT. At $243,700 before options, the Porker is just around twice as affordable.
Photo: Ferrari Mounting a motor at each corner lets the Luce meter torque independently, which is especially interesting when it comes to cornering. Equipped with 23- and 24-inch wheels, the zero-emission model further sweetens the go-faster deal with active front aero that enables a lower drag coefficient than any other Ferrari road car.
Underpinned by a dedicated EV platform, the Luce runs about two inches longer overall than the Purosangue. It also sits two inches lower. While its center of gravity is better, the high-voltage battery and its wheel-mounted electric drive units add up. The kerb weight of 2,260 kilograms (4,982 pounds) makes the Luce the heaviest Ferrari ever, and regardless of driving aids, mass will always take away some of the driving experience's quality.
Because Maranello created the Ferrari of electric vehicles with the Luce, it's hardly surprising that driving range is on the meh side. The Prancing Horse claims up to 530 kilometers (329 miles) in the WLTP from a 122-kWh structural pack that gladly takes 800 volts. Hard numbers aside, Maranello wants the Luce experienced as an electric Ferrari rather than a Ferrari doing an impression of classic models we all know and love.
Carrying one of the loudest design-focused debates in recent automotive history, the Luce wouldn't have been possible without shared input from Jony Ive and Marc Newson. Its design language isn't likely to influence Ferrari Centro Stile for the next generation of combustion and electrified models, which require a different stylistic direction to differentiate themselves from the all-electric lineup.
A car that many among us like to hate, including yours truly, the Luce is a commercial success for the time being. The entire 2026 allocation was fully spoken for in under two months after the May reveal in Rome, and the order books already cover 2027 in full. Longer term, Luce targets 2,500 deliveries by 2030, meaning 600-something units on average per annum.

CSX’s third-quarter profits increased due to a combination of volume growth, higher fuel surcharge revenue, and efficiency gains, the railroad said.
Operating income increased 44%, to $1.57 billion, while revenue increased 12%, to a record $4.02 billion, the company said Wednesday. Earnings per share increased 54%, to 57 cents. Adjusting for the impact of a one-time goodwill impairment in the third quarter of 2025, operating income was up 25% and earnings per share rose 30%.
The railroad’s (NASDAQ: CSX ) operating ratio was 60.9%, an 8.8-point improvement from a year ago, as expenses declined 2%. CSX set what it called an all-time U.S. quarterly record for fuel efficiency, at 0.92 gallons per 1,000 gross ton-miles.
Productivity improved 6% for the quarter, when measured by million gross ton-miles per employee, with overall rail employee headcount down 6.2% compared to last year.
“The progress we continue to make on productivity has helped drive substantial growth in profitability, earnings, and free cash flow. Our goal is to be the best performing railroad in North America, and the entire CSX team is responding to that challenge,” Chief Executive Steve Angel said on the railroad’s earnings call.
The results and outlook for the rest of the year prompted the railroad to raise its revenue growth forecast to high single-digits, up from prior guidance of mid-single-digit growth.
“As we move into 2027, we will be focused on ensuring we have sufficient resources across the network to support a growing business, which will include adding to our train and engine employee pipeline,” Angel said. “We remain committed to sizing our workforce to the needs of a safe, reliable, and efficient railroad.”
Overall freight volume increased 5% for the quarter. Intermodal was up 7%, merchandise was up 3%, and coal was up 2%.
The intermodal volume growth was due entirely to domestic shipments, as international traffic declined slightly.
“Reduced trucking availability, high truck rates, and elevated diesel costs continue to benefit our intermodal segment,” said Maryclare Kenney, the railroad’s chief commercial officer.
New service offerings are attracting truckloads off the highway, she said, including interline service with BNSF through Birmingham, Ala., and with CPKC through Myrtlewood, Ala. Double-stack operations, made possible by completion of the Howard Street Tunnel clearance project in Baltimore in the spring, have helped with volume growth in the I-95 Corridor.
CSX has experienced congestion at its Fairburn terminal outside Atlanta and is making investments in track, switching, and processing capacity to handle increased intermodal volume.
Export coal tonnage increased 7% for the quarter, while domestic coal tonnage declined 3% as increased metallurgical coal volume was not enough to offset a downturn in utility coal traffic.
Key operations metrics declined for the quarter amid higher volume. Average train velocity was off by 2%, while terminal dwell increased 12%, compared to a year ago.
The railroad’s service metrics declined compared to a year ago, with intermodal and carload trip-plan compliance falling 10 points each. Intermodal on-time performance was 83% for the quarter, while carload was 73%.
“We are handling more volume safely and efficiently, but we know our network can perform better,” Angel said.
Angel praised former Chief Operating Officer Mike Cory, who announced his retirement on Oct. 12. The railroad’s two operations senior vice presidents, Doug Ryhorchuk and Casey Albright, now report directly to Angel.
“Most people think of me as an operating CEO, and that’s what I like to do,” said Angel, who joined CSX a year ago after leading industrial gas company Linde. “If you go back into my early days, I actually ran manufacturing operations for GE, and I installed one of the first lean production systems in the United States back in Nineties. So operations always has been in my blood.”
Safety performance improved for the quarter, with the personal injury rate down 17% and the train accident rate down 5%. It was the seventh straight quarter of improvement in the injury rate, and the fifth consecutive quarter of improvement in the train accident rate.
Why it matters: CSX grew traffic and profits while spending less, but deteriorating service raised questions about whether its leaner operation could keep up.

2027 Hyundai Porter Drops Cab-Over Design, Super-Cab Prototype Shows Long Bed
30 photos
Photo: Baldauf
Known as the H-100 in certain markets, the fourth-generation Porter is a very old truck. Hyundai launched it 22 years ago with a distinctive cab-over design. For 2027, however, the cab-over-front-axle format is going the way of the dodo for a longer front end, resulting in a completely different profile.
Spotted in super-cab guise testing at high altitude in Europe, this full-electric prototype stops short of a conventional pickup truck hood. Its front end stops short of a conventional pickup truck hood. The camo is, unsurprisingly, thicker around the fascia and front corners, yet said camo thankfully doesn't cover the windshield.
Now sitting at a shallower angle, the windshield is joined by tall and upright side windows. The roof also runs almost flat, and each front corner exposes rectangular headlamp clusters. With the 2027 redesign, Hyundai favors a boxier aesthetic in lieu of the short and more curvaceous fascia of the outgoing model.
Adding a noticeable step between the cabin and front of the vehicle, the nose is complemented by a long bed. While a conventional pickup spreads the front structure and cab over a longer body, light commercial vehicles like this one have to balance occupant protection without giving away too much space its owner gets paid to use.
With the longer nose, the front corners shift farther away from the driver. Making the nose longer also means the front axle can be moved forward, leaving the cab slightly behind said axle without eating into the cargo area. This redesign clearly is a balancing act, and Hyundai appears to have balanced it perfectly.
Photo: Baldauf The semi-hood profile of the 2027 model gives Hyundai engineers more room to package an energy-absorbing structure, which is vital if the South Korean automaker wants to sell the next-gen Porter in the Old Continent. As with its predecessor, the biggest focus here is the bed's footprint. Such vehicles also have to work on narrow streets, and the Porter does look a lot narrower than a van-derived flatbed such as the Euro-centric Ford Transit Dropside.
As far as this prototype is concerned, the work-first priorities are especially obvious from the very plain-looking bedsides and tailgate. Its cargo area visually separates from the passenger cell, indicating a body-on-frame design engineered to handle commercial payloads. Alongside the redesigned exterior, Hyundai is also giving the Porter a techy interior and new powertrain options.
The charging connection of the super-cabbed prototype confirms full electrification, yet combustion options are clearly happening as well. Its frame reads "4WD" as well, meaning that Hyundai is considering at least one dual-motor electric powertrain. As for what actually lies inside the Porter's cab, the biggest change for 2027 is the adoption of Pleos Connect infotainment.
Regarding the rest of the dash, look forward to a modernized layout with a cleaner, more techy aesthetic, digital instrument cluster and all. The bigger question, however, is whether Hyundai can find a way to retain the center armrest seat.

Motive, an AI platform for physical operations, launched Agents on Monday at the American Trucking Associations ’ Management Conference & Exhibition (MCE) in Charlotte, North Carolina. These AI Agents act on safety and maintenance alerts under rules a fleet sets, including calling drivers, opening work orders, and bringing in managers so teams can scale without adding headcount. The company said Agents, AI that doesn’t just surface insights but acts on them, are available now to its customers. It previewed a similar rule-based tool, Automations, at its Vision 26 conference in May.
Operations teams have more visibility than ever, but they can’t act on it fast enough. The warning signs are often already in the data while acting on them still falls to managers, who chase alerts, call drivers, and check every fix by hand. That work eats hours every week and breaks down as operations grow.
For fleets, the decision rests on how much alert follow-up to hand over to software. Bennett Family of Companies, which began running Agents before the launch, started with Agents that notify its own staff and do not reach drivers.
“We did some things that did not communicate out to the drivers, and I think, for me, that was very intentional because I wanna build the trust,” Jared Whitson, senior director of safety and compliance at Bennett, said during a Motive fireside chat Sunday night at MCE. “I wanna build the trust in the product.”
Companies including Carvana, NovaSource Power, SPATCO Energy Services, Bennett Family of Companies, and Bulk Environmental & Industrial are already building and deploying Motive Agents across their operations.
What carriers already have to catch
Federal rules already make driver fatigue and vehicle condition parts of the carrier’s job. 49 CFR 392.3 bars a motor carrier from requiring or allowing a fatigued driver to operate, and 49 CFR 396.7 forbids running a truck in a condition likely to cause a crash or breakdown.
Failing to maintain that level of compliance has a direct impact on a carrier’s bottom line. Emily Parsons, a staff product manager for Agents at Motive, cited a Motive figure at the event: 47% of fleets have had delayed maintenance lead to a breakdown or an out-of-service event.
“A fault code fires, it sits in a dashboard, and by the time someone opens a ticket, a small issue oftentimes has already turned into a big one,” she said.
With Agents, a fleet picks a trigger and a response from guided workflows or ready-to-use templates in minutes, no technical expertise required, according to the release. The customer sets the threshold and the action; the Agent applies that rule continuously and consistently. Templates cover idling, fault codes, and fatigue, and one Agent can combine several triggers and actions, Motive said in a blog post .
When a fault code meets a fleet’s criteria, an Agent automatically opens a work order in Motive Maintenance and marks the vehicle out of service. Motive says each fault code comes with an AI-generated explanation, a severity level, and recommended actions.
Other agents flag driver fatigue, and idling Agents prompt drivers to shut off the engine and notify managers when idling passes a set threshold. Weather Agents can warn drivers about storms on active routes. Parsons said Motive data shows collision rates can rise as much as 40% in winter months. That is the promise of physical AI in fleet operations: connecting what hardware and software sees in the real world to what teams need done next.
“Our customers don’t need another alert. They need action,” Hemant Banavar, Motive’s chief product officer, said in the release. “The data that prevents collisions and breakdowns already lives in Motive. Agents put it to work the moment it matters, so teams can grow without adding headcount.”
Motive’s estimates and recent funding
Motive estimates organizations lose $46 billion to preventable issues such as downtime, compliance violations, and unproductive idling, and spend 860 million hours on tasks that could be automated. In the release, Motive said 42% of respondents to its 2026 ROI Report , an online survey of 351 of its North American customers, named operational inefficiencies, including excess administrative work, as a top concern.
The launch comes about six weeks after Motive raised more than $1.3 billion from General Catalyst and withdrew its IPO filing. The company said then that annual recurring revenue had passed $600 million, up 30% year over year, across nearly 100,000 customers — from small fleets to Fortune 500 enterprises — giving it one of the largest datasets in fleet management to train its AI.
Driver calls and goal setting come later
Some features are not live yet. Today, Agents alert managers by email, text, or app notification and reach drivers through in-cab voice messages, the blog post says. Calls to drivers from Atlas, Motive’s AI assistant, through AI Dashcam Plus arrive later this year.
Building an agent in plain language and setting a goal such as fewer collisions are slated for early next year. Motive also offers a library of pre-built Agents that require no setup and are available today. These Agents cover coaching and maintenance among others. Motive says Agents are included in existing Motive plans, while certain premium actions are available as add-ons. The release does not include pricing.
Bennett starts with alerts to its staff
Bennett has Motive’s AI Dashcam Plus in its vehicles but hasn’t yet enabled driver-facing Agent actions through the in-cab camera, Whitson said. Its first agent alerts asset management, the shop, and safety when a company truck with a critical fault code enters the geofence at its McDonough, Georgia, home office.
Whitson also set up an alert that notifies him when a driver logs three critical telematics events within 24 hours. Each agent is set up on a single screen: a user picks the conditions, then the action, he said. For now, Bennett’s agents report to people in the office.
Whitson noted that approach lets Bennett build confidence with back-office Agents before extending them to drivers. He said each company will decide how far to let Agents take action on its behalf. “I think it’s foolish not to make products earn that trust. But I do think that once it’s earned, then to keep up and to be competitive, then those are decisions that you’re going to have to make.”
“My team’s days are often spent running reports, cross-referencing them, and reacting to problems,” Whitson said in the press release. “Without Agents, safety management at scale is a massive challenge with inefficient, manual processes across nearly every team responsibility. Motive Agents allow us to handle that work the moment something happens — a one-time setup, and from that point forward the platform executes. Agents, and Motive’s vision for it, will let us reallocate resources toward things like field safety coordination, meaningful corrective actions, and training that ultimately lead to safer roads and money saved in collision costs.”
A scaled safety program across 15 Agents
Motive gave another customer use case example. A moving and storage company with roughly 230 vehicles is running 15 Motive Agents across its safety program. One flags patterns, including repeated speeding, unsafe lane changes, drowsiness over a rolling five-day window and auto-notifies the driver and coach when a threshold is hit. Others escalate crashes and near-misses to management by email, in-app, and SMS. The company estimates it’s saving 20 hours a week of manual event review.
HOS monitoring with a built-in buffer
A 35-vehicle fencing and guardrail contractor set up an HOS Agent that escalates as a driver nears their limit: an in-cab voice message at 60 minutes out, then a joint alert to driver and coach at 30. The 60-minute buffer gives drivers time to find safe parking and pull over legally. Most self-correct after the first message, so managers aren’t flooded with alerts. Monthly violations dropped from about 85 to 10 in September, approximately an 88% reduction.
Why it matters: A fault code that sits in a dashboard can turn into a breakdown or an out-of-service truck. Agents are built to act on those alerts automatically, closing the gap between spotting a problem and fixing it. It gives safety and maintenance teams more time for the decisions that require human judgment: field safety coordination, driver coaching, and more. Motive notes that puts them ahead of a broader industry shift from monitoring to automation.

This New Luxury Fifth Wheel RV Has Three Bedrooms, Two Bathrooms, and a Residential Feel Throughout
19 photos
Photo: Forest River/The RV Hunter
Though RVs are not built like real houses, modern units sure pack a lot of residential-grade amenities and features that make camping feel like home. And if you still think that you can't have it all in an RV, the new Sanibel 40TRIPBR luxury fifth-wheel trailer is here to prove you wrong.
The Sanibel 40TRIPBR is a new floor plan introduced by Prime Time Manufacturing, a Forest River division, for the 2027 model year and packs a lot of surprises in a towable package, including three separate bedrooms, two full bathrooms, a massive living room sofa, and even a loft.
The entire Sanibel range of luxury fifth-wheel recreational vehicles is quite appealing, comprising models ranging from 37 to 44 feet (11.2 to 13.4 meters) in length and featuring wide-body designs with multiple slide-outs and tall ceilings. Every floor plan seems designed for a specific type of traveler(s) and each promises luxury, residential-like comfort, and all the necessities for hassle-free trips.
The manufacturer has been enriching the line with some really interesting floor plans lately, but the all-new 40TRIPBR does things a bit differently. This model is clearly aimed at families who need multiple sleeping spaces and spacious communal areas, but instead of a main bedroom and a traditional bunkhouse, you get a main bedroom and two separate rear bedrooms with a loft above them. And to make things even more comfortable and convenient for families camping together, they added a second full bathroom and a separate exterior entrance.
Photo: Forest River/The RV Hunter Now you know where the name of this model came from. The TRIPBR stands for triple bedroom. But the model is so new that the company hasn’t yet got around to publishing spec details on the official website, so everything presented here is based on the video tour filmed by Hunter Megowen for his YouTube channel, which is included below.
The 2027 Sanibel 40TRIPBR is a dual-axle fifth-wheel RV with no less than five slide-outs and two entrances. Its 102-inch-wide body combined with those slide-outs creates a truly spacious interior living space. The layout puts the living room and kitchen areas in the center of the RV, flanked by the private sleeping areas at either end of the trailer.
The open-plan lounge and kitchen basically share the same area of the trailer, creating a nice gathering space for families or groups of friends. Instead of adding a regular sofa and a dedicated dinette, the builders priotized comfortable seating, so a massive five-person sofa occupies the main slide-out. It faces the kitchen and an entertainment center with a TV, soundbar, and fireplace neatly integrated above and below the counter, thus preserving valuable workspace for the kitchen.
Photo: Forest River/The RV Hunter Since there is no dinette, meals can be enjoyed at the kitchen island. And this is not just a small, regular island but a truly gorgeous one. It’s large with a breakfast bar addition and flip-up counter extension and features discreet under-cabinet LED strips. It also integrates oodles of storage, including space for trash bins, power sockets, and a workstation sink with a cup rinser, soap dispenser, and a pull-out faucet.
In the kitchen, you’ll find everything a residential kitchen is usually equipped with. It features heat-rated solid-surface countertops and real wood cabinet doors and is equipped with a four-burner cooktop, a large oven, a microwave, and a dual-door fridge/freezer. A floor-to-ceilign pantry, a separate hutch that can serve as a coffee station, and a wine rack above the microwave are also included.
Photo: Forest River/The RV Hunter The master bedroom occupies the front of the fifth-wheel, while two identical bedrooms are located at the rear, separated by a pocket door. Arranged with a king-size bed, a six-drawer dresser, a wardrobe, and a dedicated cabinet with washer and dryer prep, the main bedroom offers all the benefits you would expect from a luxury RV sleeping space. A projector and projector screen are also included, and the bed lifts up to reveal even more storage space.
The adjoining bathroom is also functional enough for a home on wheels , being fitted with a one-piece fiberglass shower, a porcelain foot-flush toilet, a stainless-steel sink, a linen closet, and a medicine cabinet.
Photo: Forest River/The RV Hunter The two rear bedrooms are basically mirroring each other. They each include a jack-knife sofa that converts into a bed, built-in wardrobe space, and a desk that holds a TV but can also be used as a desk. They are definitely more versatile than the typical bunk room found in other family-oriented designs, as they can accommodate children at night and double as study areas or office spaces during the day.
A loft stretches above these rear rooms, providing another flexible space for children to sleep or hang out. Accessed via a sturdy metal ladder, it offers about 3.5 feet (one meter) of head clearance and comes with plenty of built-in storage cubbies.
Another significant advantage of this floor plan is the inclusion of a second full bathroom at the rear. It’s smaller than the main one, it serves the two kids’ bedrooms but come with its own shower, a porcelain toilet, and a vanity. A separate rear entrance opens into this bathroom, providing direct access to the rear part of the trailer.
Photo: Forest River/The RV Hunter Like all the models in the Sanibel lineup, the 40TRIPBR features EternaBond construction, with a double-welded aluminum structure, laminated side walls, slide-outs, and roofs, and NTXT composite exterior panels. Insulated pass-through baggage doors offer access to exterior storage, including a large pass-through compartment at the front.
Key exterior features include a black glass entry door, reflective windows, two power awnings, dual 30-pound LP tanks, and a quick-connect exterior LP connection. Other standard features include a CURT Helix pin box, an electric leveling system, and tire-pressure monitoring. For climate control, the RV is equipped with a Suburban tankless water heater and furnace and a Furrion Chill Cube 18,000 BTU rooftop air conditioner.
As mentioned, Forest River has not yet published the model's official dimensions, weights, or tank capacities, but even without those details, the Sanibel 40TRIPBR fifth-wheel looks like an interesting addition to the range and it will surely appeal to families looking to share a fifth wheel without sacrificing privacy or comfortable common space.

Photo: © Eugenesergeev | Dreamstime.com
By Alison Koo
22 October 2026
Intra-Asia rates are receding from their recent highs as bottlenecks in major Chinese and other Asian ports subside.
On 15 October, Drewry’s Intra-Asia Container Index dipped 3%, to an average of $1,453 per 40ft.
Rates from Shanghai to key destinations, including Busan in South Korea, Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam, and Jawaharlal Nehru Port in India, softened as vessel waiting times declined.
The Golden Week holiday in China also gave ports an opportunity to clear cargo backlogs, helping improve schedule reliability.
Linerlytica calculated that North Asia now accounted for 37% of global port congestion, which is still the highest among all regions, but down from 50% last month.
Rates from Shanghai to Nhava Sheva fell 11%, to $3,370 per 40ft, while those to Busan declined 8% to $1,000 per 40ft. Shanghai–Singapore rates dropped 7% to $1,973 per 40ft.
Port congestion eased during Week 41, with average vessel waiting times at Busan at 23 hours, from 26 hours a week earlier. At Jawaharlal Nehru Port, waiting times declined to 24 hours, from 42, and Singapore recorded a decrease to 34 hours, from 50.
The improvement comes amid subdued demand across Greater China-to-North-east, South-east and South Asia trades, further contributing to the recent decline in spot rates.
However, the deteriorating situation in the Middle East continued to support freight rates on the Shanghai–Jebel Ali route, which remained elevated, at $8,416 per 40ft.
Elsewhere, rates across South-east and North-east Asia trade routes were largely stable, with increases recorded on those originating in Busan and Yokohama. Freight rates from Busan to Shanghai rose 4%, to $159 per 40ft, with Yokohama to Shanghai up 4%, to $120 per 40ft.
Despite the recent pullback, the intra-Asia container freight market has remained resilient this year, the IACI surging 198% year on year. Elevated bunker costs and the US–Iran tension have continued to add to carriers’ operating expenses, with Brent crude prices remaining above $100 per barrel since early September.
Meanwhile, shipping lines continue to introduce new services amid the firm market.
OOCL is set to expand its regional network tomorrow, with the launch of its China–Cambodia–Thailand (CCT4) service connecting Nansha and Shekou in South China with Sihanoukville in Cambodia and Songkhla in Thailand.
And MSC yesterday announced Jasmine, a solo China-Singapore-Indonesia service for 4 November, when the 2,169 teu MSC Wind II arrives at Shanghai. The service will call Shanghai-Ningbo-Shekou-Singapore-Surabaya-Semarang-Singapore-Shanghai.

The approval of Hibsago has created a new market for a handful of biopharmas, including Gilead, Arrowhead, and Vir, to fill in.
The approval of GSK and Ionis Pharmaceuticals’ Hibsago for chronic hepatitis B virus infection has pushed open the flood gates for a handful of followers also hoping to offer a comparable or better options for patients with the intractable disease.
Hibsago (bepirovirsen) is the first antisense oligonucleotide to receive an FDA nod for the indication. The therapy will offer a “functional cure,” meaning levels of the virus are pushed so low as to be undetectable. While partners GSK and Ionis may be the first, they won’t be the last, according to H.C. Wainwright analysts.
“The first FDA approval of an antisense oligonucleotide for chronic hepatitis B increases our confidence in the emerging functional cure market,” the firm wrote in a Thursday morning investor note. “We view approval as an important advance for the field: uncertainty over whether a finite regimen could generate sufficient sustained off-treatment responses to support FDA approval has now been resolved for bepi’s selected population.”
Behind GSK and Ionis are about 16 companies, ranging from large caps like Gilead Sciences to smaller biotechs like Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals and Aligos Therapeutics. There are also a few privately held companies like Argo Biopharmaceuticals and Tune Therapeutics in the mix.

Many of these companies will present data at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) meeting in November.
The approval of Hibsago “establishes a starting point for a multi-product market, in our view,” H.C. Wainwright wrote.
The FDA granted Hibsago approval for a fairly complex indication. The drug can be used in combination with nucleos(t)ide analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) therapy in adults with chronic hepatitis B infection who do not have liver damage. They must have been on the NRTI therapy for at least six months, have suppressed HBV DNA and have levels of hepatitis B virus (HBV) surface antigen below a certain threshold. The therapy was approved with a companion diagnostic from Roche to test for HBV surface antigen.
With such a specific population, H.C. Wainwright points out that there are plenty of patients who do not fit the exact mold. “We believe higher-antigen patients and patients who do not achieve sustained responses remain substantial opportunities for subsequent regimens.”
Aligos is one biotech that could offer such an option. The company is developing the oral capsid assembly modulator pevifoscorvir sodium (pevy) for patients with chronic infection who have a higher antigen burden. An abstract from AASLD shows a reduction in HBV surface antigen that H.C. Wainwright believes supports further exploration of whether the therapy could offer a functional cure for these patients.
Investors will have to wait until the third quarter of 2027 for a more robust Phase 2 readout from the B-SUPREME trial, which H.C. Wainwright said is “the principal pevy efficacy checkpoint.”
Precision Biosciences will also present at AASLD, showcasing Phase 1 results from the ELIMINATE-B program for the gene therapy PBGENE-HBV. While the data are early, H.C. Wainwright will be watching for details on the duration of pgRNA loss, which is the biomarker Precision is tracking to look for the elimination of the stable viral genomes that give rise to new HBV infections.
GSK and Ionis will also have a showing at AASLD. H.C. Wainwright expects the presentation to help physicians understand how to select and manage patients.
Arrowhead is another company that could benefit from the new market established by Ionis and GSK. The biotech’s siRNA daplusiran/tomligisiran is being tested by GSK in the Phase 2b B-UNITED trial along with Hibsago.
Assembly Biosciences, which is developing the oral hepatitis D virus (HDV) entry inhibitor ABI-6250, is a “partnering opportunity,” according to H.C. Wainwright.
Other names with early assets include Vir Biotechnology’s elebsiran and tobevibart combo and Mirum Pharmaceuticals’ monoclonal antibody brelovitug . “We would not transfer bepi’s HBV approval directly into higher efficacy assumptions for those programs,” H.C. Wainwright said.
